lesson_text: A stock is trending when price sits above its 20-day moving average, the 20-day sits above the 50-day, and the 50-day sits above the 200-day, with the averages sloping up. The desk's screener labels this stack full-bull every night. On the chart it shows as higher highs and higher lows with pullbacks that hold the rising averages. The screener's test is the three-average stack. A trader reads the same thing from the swings: as long as each pullback bottoms above the last one, the trend is intact. It depends on the timeframe you are looking at: a stock can be in an uptrend on the weekly and pulling back on the daily at the same time, and the desk reads the longer frame first.

lesson_text: The last several closes are bunched together in a narrow band: the daily ranges have shrunk and the stock is going sideways in a small box. The desk's screener calls a stock tight when the spread of its last ten closes is under 2.5% of price. A coiled stock has stored energy; the next expansion in range is the move, up or down. Tightness is a measurement, not a direction. It matters most when it comes after a strong move (a flag) or near the top of a base, because the holders who wanted out have left and the ones who remain are not selling. Coiled on light volume is the classic look; coiled on heavy volume means a fight.

lesson_text: Each pullback bottoms above the one before it. Buyers are stepping in earlier every time, which is the simplest proof an uptrend is alive. The desk's screener counts a run of three or more consecutive higher lows as the pattern. Draw a line under the lows and it slopes up; that line is the trend line the desk watches. The moment a pullback undercuts the previous low, the sequence is broken and the trend is in doubt. Higher lows into a flat high is a tightening wedge, often a breakout waiting to happen.

lesson_text: A day whose entire range sits inside the previous day's range: a lower high and a higher low. Nothing was decided that day. After a strong move, an inside day is a pause; the break of the two-day high or low is the next decision. The desk reads an inside day after a big up day as a sign the stock is holding its gains quietly, which is what it wants to see before a continuation. Several inside days stacked up are a coil. The same bar after a big down day is just as meaningful in the other direction.

lesson_text: The stock opens well away from where it closed. If it never trades back into the prior day's range, it leaves empty space on the chart between the two days. The desk's screener calls it gapping when the open is 3% or more above (or below) the prior close. Gaps come from news that arrived while the market was shut: earnings, guidance, a deal, an upgrade. The gap itself is not the trade; what the stock does with the gap is. A gap up on earnings that holds its opening range and keeps going on heavy volume is a Power Earnings Gap; a gap up that fades back into the prior day's range is a failure. Gap support, where the bottom of the gap holds on the next pullback, is one of the desk's levels.

lesson_text: Far more shares changed hands than usual for that stock. The desk's screener calls it heavy when the day's volume is at least twice the stock's own average. Volume is the footprint of institutions: a breakout on heavy volume has real buyers behind it, a breakout on thin volume is a rumour. Heavy is always relative to the stock's own average, never an absolute number; two million shares is huge for one name and nothing for another. The direction matters as much as the amount: heavy volume on an up day is accumulation, heavy volume on a down day is distribution. The High Volume Close setup is built on this word.

lesson_text: The stock is trading within 5% of its highest price of the past year. A stock near its highs has little overhead supply: most people who bought it in the past year are in profit, so there are few trapped holders waiting to sell into strength. At new highs means it printed a fresh 52-week high today. The desk buys strength, so near the highs is where it shops, in a market that allows it. The opposite, a stock far below its highs, carries overhead supply at every level it fell through. The 52-week high is the standard lookback; a stock near all-time highs is the same idea with no supply at all above it.

lesson_text: The stock is within 2% of its 20-day exponential moving average, above or below. The 20 EMA is the desk's short-term trend line: in a healthy uptrend the stock rides above it and touches it on pullbacks, so a leader sitting at the 20 is a leader at a decision point. The screener's band is plus or minus 2%. The 20-day exponential average weights recent closes more than a simple average does, so it hugs price more closely. Being at the 20 is only interesting when the average is rising and the stock is above its 50-day; at a falling 20 EMA the same touch is resistance, not support.

lesson_text: A short move against the trend: in an uptrend, a few days of selling that bring the stock back toward its moving averages before the trend resumes. The desk calls a pullback shallow when it gives back 5% or less from the recent high and deep when it gives back 20% or more. A pullback that holds a rising 20-day or 50-day average is where many of the desk's entries live. Shallow and deep are the screener's two thresholds (5% and 20%). In between is just a pullback. What makes a pullback buyable is not the depth alone but how it behaves: orderly, on lighter volume, holding the average, then turning back up. A pullback on heavy volume that slices through the 50-day is a different animal.
